items.title: Goldsboro Revisited
items.summary: A two-page 1969 memo by Sandia weapons safety supervisor Parker F. Jones about the January 1961 B-52 breakup over North Carolina, which dropped two Mark 39 hydrogen bombs near Goldsboro. Jones concluded that the bomb lacked adequate safety for the B-52 airborne alert role and that one low-voltage switch stood between the United States and a major catastrophe.

facts.claim: The B-52 broke up over North Carolina on 23-24 January 1961 and released two Mark 39 Mod 2 thermonuclear bombs over farmland at Faro, near Goldsboro.
Parker F. Jones, supervisor of the nuclear weapons safety department at Sandia, wrote the document in 1969 and said one low-voltage switch stood between the United States and a major catastrophe.
Eric Schlosser came upon the newly declassified memo while researching Command and Control and gave it to The Guardian, which published it on 20 September 2013.
The National Archives shows both pages of the Jones memo, credited to the Records of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff.

items.title: Hardtack I: Nutmeg test film
items.summary: Color film of Nutmeg, a 25-kiloton Livermore test device fired on a barge at Bikini Atoll on 22 May 1958 during Operation Hardtack I. Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory declassified the film and posted it online in March 2017, in a project to save decaying nuclear test films.

facts.claim: Nutmeg was a 25.1-kiloton barge shot at Eninmen, Bikini Atoll, fired at 21:20 UTC on 21 May 1958 (22 May local time).
In March 2017 LLNL published an initial set of declassified films of its own tests in a YouTube playlist, from about 10,000 test films that were decomposing in vaults.
LLNL's YouTube channel published 'Operation Hardtack-1 - Nutmeg 51538' on 13 March 2017.

items.title: Project A119: Lunar Research Flights
items.summary: Volume I of a 1959 study by Leonard Reiffel of the Armour Research Foundation for the Air Force Special Weapons Center on what a nuclear explosion near the Moon could reveal; Carl Sagan is listed as a contributor. The plan, later known as Project A119, was never carried out and became publicly known when Reiffel described it in 2000.
items.credit: L. Reiffel, Armour Research Foundation, for the Air Force Special Weapons Center

facts.claim: Report AFSWC-TR-59-39 Volume 1, by L. Reiffel of the Armour Research Foundation, is dated 19 June 1959 and has 190 pages (DTIC AD0425380).
The report considers nuclear detonations in the vicinity of the Moon and the scientific information they could give.
Reiffel revealed the project in 2000, and Volume I was made public after a freedom of information request that followed.

items.title: Trinity Fireball at 16 ms
items.summary: Berlyn Brixner's photograph of the Trinity fireball 0.016 seconds after the first nuclear explosion, in New Mexico on 16 July 1945. Fireball photos with elapsed times were declassified in July 1947, and physicist G. I. Taylor later used them to estimate the bomb's yield.
items.credit: Berlyn Brixner, Los Alamos National Laboratory

facts.claim: Los Alamos photo PA-98-0520 by Berlyn Brixner shows the Trinity explosion 0.016 seconds after detonation on 16 July 1945.
Fireball photos printed in August 1945 had no time stamps; high-quality images with elapsed times were released when the AEC declassified Julian Mack's report on 17 July 1947.
G. I. Taylor used the Mack photos to estimate the yield at 17 to 24 kilotons.

items.title: Operation Ivy
items.summary: Silent 10-minute National Archives reel of Operation Ivy, the Air Force film of Mike, the first full-scale hydrogen bomb test, with actor Reed Hadley as host. Mike yielded 10.4 megatons on 1 November 1952 and left a crater where the island of Elugelab had been; a censored version of the film was released to the public in 1954.
items.credit: U.S. Air Force (Lookout Mountain film unit) for Joint Task Force 132

facts.claim: Mike was fired on 1 November 1952 at 07:15 local time, yielded 10.4 megatons and left a crater 1.9 km wide where Elugelab had been.
The film, hosted by Reed Hadley, was released to the public after censoring in 1954 and shown on commercial television.
The National Archives holds this silent reel (NAID 66458, 342-USAF-21553, dated 2 February 1954), produced by the Department of the Air Force.

items.title: SAC Atomic Weapons Requirements Study
items.summary: Title page, contents and introduction of Strategic Air Command's June 1956 study of the atomic weapons it would need for a war in 1959. The full study listed more than 1,100 Soviet bloc airfields and more than 1,200 cities as targets, with 'population' as a target in cities such as Moscow, Leningrad, East Berlin, Warsaw and Beijing.
items.credit: U.S. Air Force, Strategic Air Command

facts.claim: The SAC Atomic Weapons Requirements Study for 1959 was produced in June 1956, runs to more than 800 pages and was published by the National Security Archive on 22 December 2015.
It lists more than 1,100 airfields and over 1,200 cities in the Soviet bloc, and it targeted 'population' in cities including Beijing, Moscow, Leningrad, East Berlin and Warsaw.
The National Archives declassified it after a 2006 Mandatory Declassification Review request from journalist Michael Dobbs and told him in October 2014.

items.title: Castle Bravo
items.summary: Aerial photograph of the Castle Bravo fireball over Bikini Atoll on 1 March 1954, the largest nuclear test the United States ever conducted. Bravo yielded 15 megatons, nearly three times what its planners expected, and its fallout sickened Marshall Islanders and contaminated 23 Japanese fishermen.
items.credit: Defense Atomic Support Agency, National Archives (RG 374)

facts.claim: Castle Bravo was fired on 1 March 1954, yielded 15 megatons, nearly three times the 6 megatons its planners expected, gravely sickened Marshall Islanders and contaminated 23 Japanese fishermen.
The National Archives catalogs this print as 'Bravo Fireball, Aerial View' in Project 22, Operation Castle.
The photo series is marked declassified and came to the National Archives under accession NN3-374-93-001.

items.title: Starfish Prime
items.summary: Photograph of the Starfish Prime burst and the aurora it made, taken from atop Haleakala on Maui. The 1.4-megaton warhead exploded about 400 km above the Pacific near Johnston Atoll on 9 July 1962, and its electromagnetic pulse knocked out about 300 streetlights in Hawaii.
items.credit: Defense Atomic Support Agency, National Archives (RG 374)

facts.claim: The National Archives describes this photo as 'Starfish burst and aurora from atop Haleakala crater, Maui' (374-ANT-26-14420-62).

Starfish Prime was a 1.4-megaton W49 warhead launched on a Thor rocket from Johnston Atoll and detonated about 400 km up on 9 July 1962 (UTC); its EMP knocked out about 300 streetlights in Hawaii, about 1,450 km away.
The photo series is marked declassified and came to the National Archives under accession NN3-374-93-001.
